title: Reconstruction, 1865–1877
summary: Students trace Reconstruction from the end of the Civil War to the Compromise of 1877. They read primary sources, debate whether it failed in a Socratic seminar, and write a document-based essay.
brief: Reconstruction for grade 11 US history: eight 50-minute lessons from the end of the Civil War to the Compromise of 1877: Lincoln's and Johnson's plans, the Freedmen's Bureau, the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments, Black Codes, Radical Reconstruction, the rise of the Ku Klux Klan and the end of Reconstruction. Use short primary-source excerpts in every lesson, a Socratic seminar on whether Reconstruction failed, and a document-based essay at the end (50%). Seminar 20%, lesson exit tickets 30%.
policies:
This unit includes sources that describe racial violence and use the language of their time. We read them as evidence. When a source prints a slur or another offensive term for race, the teacher says “the slur” or skips the word, and students never say it aloud. Anyone may step out for a moment without asking.

An exit ticket is collected every lesson and scored from 0 to 3: 3 for every part correct, 2 for most parts correct, 1 for an attempt with a major gap, 0 if not handed in. The eight scores add up to a mark out of 24, which is the exit-ticket grade (30%). A missed ticket cannot be made up without an excused absence.

The document-based essay is submitted on paper or through the class site by the start of class on the due date; late essays lose 5% a day.

Quote and cite the documents we read in class. Wording copied from anywhere without quotation marks is plagiarism.

segments.title: A defeated South: what must be settled?
segments.description:
Give the date facts on the board: Lee surrendered at Appomattox on April 9, 1865, and Lincoln died on April 15 after being shot the night before.
Students write three questions the country must answer now that the war is over.
They share one question with a partner and star the one they think is most urgent.
Collect a few on the board for use later in the class.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect: Who is in charge? Can Confederate states rejoin? Will leaders be punished? What happens to freed people? Keep the list on the board for the discussion segment.

segments.title: Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan
segments.description:
Explain the Proclamation of Amnesty and Reconstruction of December 1863. Confederates who swore an oath of loyalty and accepted emancipation received a pardon and their property back, except enslaved people.
High Confederate officials and top army officers were excluded from the pardon.
When 10 percent of a state’s 1860 voters had taken the oath, the state could form a government. Louisiana did so in 1864.
Note that Congress disliked the plan as too lenient and passed the Wade-Davis Bill, which required a majority and a stricter oath. Lincoln pocket-vetoed it in July 1864.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: thinking 10 percent of the current population. It was 10 percent of 1860 voters, who were white men only. Ask students who that left out.

segments.title: Reading Lincoln’s Second Inaugural
segments.description:
Hand out two excerpts from Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address (March 4, 1865): the opening of the paragraph beginning “One-eighth of the whole population were colored slaves”, as far as “somehow the cause of the war”, and the final paragraph beginning “With malice toward none”.
Students read each silently and underline what Lincoln says caused the war in the first excerpt.
In the second, they underline what he asks of the nation after the war.
Pairs write one sentence on what each excerpt suggests about how Lincoln wanted to treat the South.
segments.teacherNotes: Prepare copies of both excerpts. First excerpt: slavery was a powerful interest that everyone knew was the war’s cause. Second: no malice, finish the work, bind up wounds, lasting peace. The first excerpt uses the period term “colored”. Students read it on the page and do not say it; in discussion everyone says “Black people” or “enslaved people”.

segments.title: Johnson’s pardon-based plan
segments.description:
Explain that Andrew Johnson, Lincoln’s vice president, became president and issued his Amnesty Proclamation on May 29, 1865, while Congress was out of session until December.
Most Southerners received a pardon and their property back (not enslaved people) by swearing an oath.
Confederate officials and anyone with taxable property over $20,000 had to apply to Johnson personally.
Johnson appointed provisional governors. Johnson required states to void secession, abolish slavery, ratify the 13th Amendment and repudiate Confederate debt. His plan set no required share of voters and did not require voting rights for Black men. He recognized restored state governments, but Congress refused to seat their elected representatives.
segments.teacherNotes: Stress that Johnson granted thousands of individual pardons, so planters regained political power fast. Common mistake: calling Johnson a Republican; he was a Southern Democrat on Lincoln’s 1864 Union ticket.

segments.title: Lincoln, Johnson or both?
segments.description:
In pairs, students get five statements and label each Lincoln, Johnson or both, using their notes.
They circle the statement that most helped former Confederates return to power.
Review the answers together and correct notes as needed.
segments.teacherNotes:
Read each aloud or write on the board. 1. A state could form a government once 10 percent of its 1860 voters swore loyalty. Lincoln.
2. Rich Confederates with over $20,000 in taxable property had to ask the president personally for a pardon. Johnson.
3. Southerners had to accept the end of slavery. Both.
4. The plan was announced while Congress was out of session until December. Johnson.
5. High Confederate officials were excluded from the general pardon. Both.

segments.title: What did Reconstruction have to settle?
segments.description:
Return to the warmup questions on the board.
As a class, sort them into four groups: who controls Reconstruction, terms for readmitting states, who is pardoned or punished, and the rights of freed people.
Ask which questions remained unresolved, especially who controls Reconstruction and what rights freed people would have beyond freedom from slavery.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: neither plan gave Black men the vote, citizenship or land. Name that the president acted alone, so the struggle between president and Congress is a question, not an answer, going into the lessons ahead.

segments.title: Exit ticket
segments.description:
Students answer on a half sheet and hand it in.
Question: A Georgia planter fought as a private and owns $40,000 in taxable property. In summer 1865, what must he do to be pardoned under Johnson’s plan? Would Lincoln’s plan have treated him differently? Then name one question about the freed people that neither plan settled.
segments.teacherNotes: Counts toward the lesson exit tickets component (30% of the course grade). Score it 0–3: 3 for every part correct, 2 for most parts correct, 1 for an attempt with a major gap, 0 if not handed in. Expected: he swears the oath and applies personally to Johnson for a pardon because his property exceeds $20,000. Under Lincoln, the oath alone would pardon him as a private. Neither settled: citizenship, voting or land for freed people.

keyIdeas: Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan let a Confederate state form a new government once 10 percent of its 1860 voters swore loyalty to the Union and accepted the end of slavery.

Andrew Johnson’s plan, announced in May 1865, rested on presidential pardons: most Southerners swore an oath, wealthy and high-ranking ones had to apply to him personally, and states formed governments under appointed provisional governors.
Both plans were made by the president alone, without Congress, and both left open the rights of the four million freed people.
In 1865 the country had to settle who controls Reconstruction, on what terms Confederate states return, who is punished or pardoned, and what freedom means for formerly enslaved people.

study.overview: After the Civil War ended in April 1865, the country had to decide how the defeated South would return to the Union. Two presidents made two different plans, both on their own. Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan was lenient and tied to an oath and the end of slavery. Andrew Johnson’s plan relied on individual pardons and let planters regain power quickly. Neither plan settled what freedom would mean for four million freed people.

points.heading: Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan
points.explanation: Lincoln’s Proclamation of Amnesty and Reconstruction (December 1863) offered a pardon and the return of property, except enslaved people, to Confederates who swore an oath of loyalty and accepted the end of slavery. High Confederate officials and top army officers were excluded. Once 10 percent of a state’s 1860 voters had taken the oath, the state could form a new government. Note that this means 10 percent of 1860 voters, not of the whole population, and those voters were white men only. Louisiana formed a government this way in 1864. Congress thought the plan too lenient and passed the Wade-Davis Bill, which required a majority of voters and a stricter oath. Lincoln pocket-vetoed it in July 1864. His Second Inaugural (March 4, 1865) fits this approach: he asked the nation to act ‘with malice toward none’ and to bind up the nation’s wounds.

points.heading: Johnson’s pardon-based plan
points.explanation: Andrew Johnson became president after Lincoln died on April 15, 1865. He had been Lincoln’s vice president on the 1864 Union ticket, but he was a Southern Democrat, not a Republican. His Amnesty Proclamation of May 29, 1865, came while Congress was out of session until December. Most Southerners received a pardon and their property back, except enslaved people, by swearing an oath. Confederate officials and anyone with taxable property over $20,000 had to apply to Johnson personally. He appointed provisional governors and required states to void secession, abolish slavery, ratify the 13th Amendment and repudiate Confederate debt. He set no required share of voters and did not require voting rights for Black men. Because he granted thousands of individual pardons, planters regained political power fast. Example: a Virginia planter who fought as a private and owned $30,000 in taxable property had to swear the oath and also apply to Johnson personally for a pardon. Under Lincoln’s plan, the oath alone would have pardoned him.

points.heading: What neither plan settled
points.explanation: Both plans were made by the president alone, without Congress, and both left open the rights of the four million freed people. Neither gave Black men the vote, citizenship or land. Johnson’s restored state governments were recognized by him, but Congress refused to seat their elected representatives. This left a struggle between president and Congress still to come.

points.heading: The four questions of 1865
points.explanation: In 1865 the country had to settle four things. Who controls Reconstruction: the president or Congress? On what terms do Confederate states return? Who is punished or pardoned? What does freedom mean for formerly enslaved people, beyond freedom from slavery? You can use these questions to sort any event you study later. For example, Johnson’s pardons answer the third question, while the missing voting rights for Black men leave the fourth unanswered.

l_b74a9e6258d8.title: The Freedmen's Bureau and the 13th Amendment
l_b74a9e6258d8.summary: Students examine what the Freedmen's Bureau did for schools, labor contracts and land, and how the 13th Amendment ended slavery; they read a report by the Bureau's commissioner and complete an exit ticket.

segments.title: What does freedom need?
segments.description:
Return to the question left open on the board last time: what rights freed people would have beyond freedom from slavery.
Students imagine a freed family in Georgia in summer 1865. On an index card they list three things the family needs in order to live free.
They share the list with a partner and circle one need that a government would have to supply.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect: food, work for pay, land, schools, protection from violence, legal rights. Keep the circled needs on the board. The next segment sorts them into schools, labor contracts and land.

segments.title: What the Freedmen’s Bureau did
segments.description:
Explain that Congress created the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands on March 3, 1865, under the War Department, with General Oliver O. Howard as commissioner.
Teach its three main functions. Schools: it worked with Northern aid societies and Black communities to open thousands of schools. Labor contracts: agents helped freed people negotiate written work agreements and settle wage disputes. Land: General Sherman’s Special Field Order No. 15 of January 1865 set aside coastal land from South Carolina to northern Florida in 40-acre plots, and the Bureau was to manage abandoned land.
Students match the needs on their cards to the three functions.
Close by telling them that President Johnson’s pardons in fall 1865 returned most of this land to its former owners.
segments.teacherNotes: Misconception: that every freed person got 40 acres and a mule. Most got none, and the land was returned. Point out that Black communities paid for and built many schools themselves. For scale: no more than about 900 agents served across the whole South at any one time.

segments.title: The 13th Amendment and its exception clause
segments.description:
Show how the amendment moved from passage by the Senate in April 1864 and the House in January 1865 to ratification on December 6, 1865. Remind students that Johnson required the Southern states to ratify it.
Put an excerpt from Section 1 on the board and read it aloud: “Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States […]”
Explain that it ended slavery everywhere, including the border states, and that Section 2 gave Congress power to enforce it.
Ask students to underline the words that make an exception.
segments.teacherNotes: Point out that the clause covers only people “duly convicted” of a crime. Next time, the Black Codes will show how states used it, so only flag it now.

segments.title: What changed and what did not
segments.description:
In pairs, students read the four cases on the board and decide for each: banned by the 13th Amendment, allowed by the exception clause, or unclear.
They write the words of Section 1 that support each answer.
Review the answers as a class and correct notes as needed.
segments.teacherNotes:
Cases, with answers:
1. A planter keeps a family working without pay and calls them his property. Banned: slavery.
2. A man tried and convicted of theft is sentenced to hard labor. Allowed by the exception clause: duly convicted.
3. A planter forces a worker to stay by threatening to beat him. Banned: forcing a worker to stay through threats is involuntary servitude. No punishment following a criminal conviction is described.
4. A state wants to keep slavery within its borders. Banned: applies to the whole United States.
Common mistake: reading the clause as covering any arrest.

segments.title: Reading a Bureau commissioner’s report: how much power?
segments.description:
Hand out a passage of about 150 words from Maj. Gen. Oliver O. Howard’s annual report for 1866 as commissioner of the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands. Choose a passage in which Howard reports on the officers and agents on duty and on the Bureau’s need for troops.
Students read the excerpt and annotate it. They circle what Howard says the Bureau could do and bracket what it needed from others.
In pairs, they write two sentences answering: how much power did the Bureau really have?
segments.teacherNotes:
Prepare copies with the report’s title, author and year printed above the passage. Howard was commissioner, so say plainly that he reports for the Bureau and had reason to show its work well. Questions, with answers expected depending on the passage chosen:
1. What does Howard report about the officers and agents the Bureau had? Expect: students point to the staffing detail in the passage and explain why it suggests agents were spread thin. For scale, no more than about 900 served across the South at one time.
2. Who enforced its decisions? Expect: army officers and troops.
3. What does that mean when troops leave? Expect: the Bureau’s power shrinks.
If the passage does not answer a question, give the answer yourself rather than asking students to find it.

segments.title: Powerful or limited?
segments.description:
Hold a quick whole-class discussion: did the Bureau have the power to protect freedom, or only the duty?
Students use the report and the land reversal as evidence of limits on Bureau power. They distinguish these limits from the exception clause, which limits the amendment’s ban on forced labor.
Each student states one limit on Bureau power in a sentence to a neighbor.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect limits: few agents, reliance on the army, Johnson’s return of land, and later Johnson’s veto of a Bureau extension bill in February 1866. Congress failed to override that veto, but passed a revised bill and overrode his veto of that bill in July 1866. Accept either side with evidence.

segments.title: Exit ticket
segments.description:
Students answer on a half sheet and hand it in.
Question: Name three things the Freedmen’s Bureau did. Then explain what the 13th Amendment’s exception clause allowed, and give one reason the Bureau’s power was limited. Answer in three or four sentences.
segments.teacherNotes: Counts toward the lesson exit tickets component (30% of the course grade). Score it 0–3: 3 for every part correct, 2 for most parts correct, 1 for an attempt with a major gap, 0 if not handed in. Expected: schools, labor contracts and land (accept other real Bureau work, such as food relief or medical care); involuntary servitude stayed legal as punishment for a crime after due conviction; few agents, reliance on the army, or Johnson returning land.

keyIdeas: Congress created the Freedmen’s Bureau in March 1865 to help formerly enslaved people with schools, labor contracts and land. Its head was General Oliver O. Howard.
The Bureau built schools and helped freed people negotiate work contracts. It helped freed people settle on abandoned land, but Johnson’s 1865 pardons returned much of that land to former owners.
The 13th Amendment, ratified December 6, 1865, ended slavery across the United States. Its exception clause allowed involuntary servitude as punishment for crime.
The Bureau had few agents and depended on the army and on the president’s support. Both were uncertain, so its power was limited.

vocabulary.definition: The federal agency, created in March 1865 within the War Department, that helped formerly enslaved people with schools, labor contracts and land.
A written agreement between a worker and an employer that sets the work, the pay and the length of service.

The words in the 13th Amendment that allow involuntary servitude as punishment for a crime of which a person has been duly convicted.

Congress failed to override that veto, but passed a revised bill and overrode his veto of that bill in July 1866. Each student states one limit in a sentence to a neighbor.

bullets: Name three things the Freedmen’s Bureau did.
Explain what the 13th Amendment’s exception clause allowed.

Write three or four sentences on a half sheet.
slides.notes: About 5 minutes. Students answer on a half sheet and hand it in. The exit ticket counts toward the lesson exit tickets component, which is 30% of the course grade. study.overview: The Freedmen’s Bureau was created by Congress on March 3, 1865, to help formerly enslaved people build free lives. General Oliver O. Howard was its commissioner. The 13th Amendment, ratified on December 6, 1865, ended slavery across the United States, but it left one exception. Both the Bureau and the amendment mattered, and both had limits. This guide reviews what each did and where each fell short.

points.heading: Three jobs of the Freedmen’s Bureau
points.explanation: The Bureau worked in three main areas. Schools: it worked with Northern aid societies and Black communities to open thousands of schools. Black communities also paid for and built many schools themselves. Labor contracts: agents helped freed people negotiate written work agreements and settle wage disputes. Land: General Sherman’s Special Field Order No. 15 of January 1865 set aside coastal land from South Carolina to northern Florida in 40-acre plots, and the Bureau was to manage abandoned land. Example: think of the freed family in Georgia in summer 1865. A need for schooling points to the Bureau’s schools. A need for fair pay points to its work on contracts. A need for a farm points to its land role.

points.heading: Land: a promise that mostly did not hold
points.explanation: Many people think every freed person received 40 acres and a mule. That is not true. Most freed people got no land. President Johnson’s pardons in fall 1865 returned most of the abandoned land to its former owners. Example: a family that had settled on coastal land under Sherman’s order could lose it when the former owner received a pardon. The Bureau could help people settle on land, but it could not keep that land from being returned.

points.heading: The 13th Amendment and its exception clause
points.explanation: Congress passed the amendment in the Senate in April 1864 and the House in January 1865. It was ratified on December 6, 1865. Johnson required the Southern states to ratify it. Section 1 reads: “Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States […]” It ended slavery everywhere, including the border states. Section 2 gave Congress power to enforce it. The exception covers only people “duly convicted” of a crime. It does not cover any arrest. Example: a man tried and convicted of theft and sentenced to hard labor falls under the exception. A planter who forces a worker to stay by threatening to beat him does not. That is involuntary servitude with no criminal conviction. Next time, you will see how some states used this clause.

points.heading: Why the Bureau’s power was limited
points.explanation: The Bureau had few agents. It depended on the army and on the president’s support, and both were uncertain. Howard’s annual report for 1866, which you read in class, shows how much the Bureau relied on army officers and troops. If troops left, the Bureau’s power shrank. Johnson’s return of land is another limit. So is his veto of a Bureau extension bill in February 1866. Congress failed to override that veto. It then passed a revised bill and overrode his veto of that bill in July 1866. Keep these limits separate from the exception clause. The Bureau’s limits were about enforcement. The exception clause limits the amendment’s ban on forced labor. Example: few agents, reliance on the army and Johnson’s return of land are each a reason the Bureau’s power was limited.

l_9cbdc67cd227.title: Black Codes and the Civil Rights Act of 1866
l_9cbdc67cd227.summary: Students analyze Mississippi's 1865 Black Code and Congress's response in the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and Johnson's veto; an exit ticket closes the class.

segments.title: What could the exception clause allow?
segments.description:
Display the words of the 13th Amendment’s exception clause from last time: involuntary servitude is allowed as punishment for a crime.
Students write two sentences. The first says how a Southern legislature that wanted to control Black workers might use that clause. The second says what kind of law it would need to pass.
Two students read answers aloud. Tell the class they will test these predictions against real laws today.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: pass laws that make ordinary acts crimes for Black people, then force the convicted to work. Do not reveal Mississippi’s laws yet. Ask for predictions about legislatures, not about any person.

segments.title: The Black Codes in Mississippi
segments.description:
Explain that in late 1865 governments formed under Johnson’s plan passed Black Codes, and Mississippi’s laws of November 1865 were among the first.
Show that the laws gave some rights: owning personal property, suing in court and legal marriage.
Show that they also restricted work, family life and weapons, while Johnson’s plan had required no vote or citizenship for Black men.
Set the task: in the next segment pairs will read the laws themselves and sort what they restrict.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: thinking the codes said “slavery”. They explicitly named Black people and imposed racial restrictions. The vagrancy provision also punished white people for specified associations with Black people. Naming the laws as written is not the same as endorsing them. The texts use period terms for race such as “negroes” and “mulattoes”. Follow the course rule: say they are the legislature’s words, skip them if you read a line aloud, and have students read them on the page without saying them. In discussion everyone says “Black people”.

segments.title: Sorting the Mississippi restrictions
segments.description:
Hand out four labeled excerpts, each stating the act and section it comes from. Pairs read each excerpt silently and underline who it applies to and what it requires or forbids.
Pairs sort the four restrictions on the board into four groups: control of work, control of children and family, forced labor after a fine, and weapons.
Pairs then circle the one restriction that most closely uses the exception clause from the warm-up and write one sentence saying why.
segments.teacherNotes:
Prepare copies of four short excerpts from Laws of Mississippi, 1865. (1) “An Act to confer Civil Rights on Freedmen, and for other purposes,” Sections 4-6, with Section 5 (home or employment) marked. (2) “An Act to regulate the relation of master and apprentice, as relates to freedmen, free negroes, and mulattoes,” Section 1. (3) “An Act to amend the vagrant laws of the state,” Sections 2 and 5. (4) “An Act to punish certain offences therein named, and for other purposes,” Section 1. Trim for length and label each excerpt.
Board items and answers:
1. Black adults must show a lawful home or employment, with written proof each year (civil rights act, Sec. 5): control of work.
2. Black minors can be bound to an employer when parents are judged unable or unwilling to support them, even if the parents are alive; former owner preferred (apprenticeship act, Sec. 1): children and family.
3. Black adults with no lawful employment or business can be fined, and if they cannot pay they are hired out (vagrancy act, Secs. 2 and 5): forced labor after a fine. This is the exception clause in use.
4. Black people may not keep or carry firearms or bowie knives without a license (offenses act, Sec. 1): weapons.
Be exact: the vagrancy act covered adults with no lawful employment or business, not every adult without papers. Treat the apprenticeship of children with care. Do not ask students to take the part of those bound or those who bound them.

segments.title: Northern anger and the Civil Rights Act
segments.description:
Explain that many Northerners saw the codes as slavery in new form. Note that Georgia’s legislature elected Alexander Stephens, the former Confederate vice president, to the Senate in 1866, and Congress refused to seat Southern members.
Hand out Section 1 of the Civil Rights Act of 1866. Read it aloud once and explain that it defined citizenship and listed equal rights.
Pairs identify Section 1 guarantees that challenge the Mississippi restrictions from the last segment and explain each connection. A restriction may connect to several guarantees, and some guarantees may have no direct match in these excerpts. They then name one restriction the section does not clearly address.
segments.teacherNotes: Prepare copies of the Civil Rights Act of 1866, Section 1, beginning “That all persons born in the United States”. Expected matches: the right to make and enforce contracts answers the home-or-employment rule; full and equal benefit of laws for the security of person and property answers the firearms ban; equal punishment answers fines and hiring out. Apprenticeship is not clearly addressed. Accept reasoned arguments. Congress passed the act in March 1866.

segments.title: Reading Johnson’s veto
segments.description:
Hand out three marked passages from Johnson’s veto message of March 27, 1866, labeled A, B and C. Read each aloud once.
Students write one sentence in their own words for each passage, saying what Johnson objects to and why.
Tell the class that Congress overrode the veto in April 1866, the first time it did so on a major law. Students write what that suggests about who controls Reconstruction.
segments.teacherNotes: Prepare copies of Andrew Johnson, Veto of the Civil Rights Bill (March 27, 1866). Mark three short passages. (A) The two sentences from “They interfere with the municipal legislation of the States” to “concentration of all legislative powers in the National Government”. (B) The sentence beginning “If, on the other hand, such persons are not citizens”. (C) The two sentences right after it, beginning “Four millions of them have just emerged from slavery into freedom”. Expected: A the bill takes over power that belongs to the states, B eleven states had no representatives in Congress, C people just out of slavery are being made citizens too fast. Passage B uses the period term “colored”; skip it when you read aloud, under the course rule. Say that these are Johnson’s arguments; students restate them and need not agree. Override: Senate April 6, House April 9.

segments.title: Did Congress answer the Black Codes?
segments.description:
Ask the class whether the Civil Rights Act answered the restrictions they sorted. Students cite one restriction from the sorting and one guarantee from Section 1.
Return to the board questions about who controls Reconstruction and what rights freed people would have. Ask which question the override helped settle.
segments.teacherNotes: Accept either answer if it cites evidence. Expected gaps: apprenticeship and enforcement. Name that a law can be repealed or ignored, leaving the question open going into the lessons ahead. Redirect any students who generalize about all Southerners to name specific laws or officials.

segments.title: Exit ticket
segments.description:
Students answer on a half sheet and hand it in.
Question: Name one restriction in Mississippi’s 1865 laws. Explain why many Northerners were angry about the Black Codes. Then give one reason Johnson vetoed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and say what Congress did next.
Collect before the bell.
segments.teacherNotes: Counts toward the lesson exit tickets component (30% of the course grade). Score it 0–3: 3 for every part correct, 2 for most parts correct, 1 for an attempt with a major gap, 0 if not handed in. Expected: a restriction (work proof, apprenticeship, vagrancy fine and hiring out, or weapons ban); anger because the codes looked like slavery after Union victory; a reason (state authority, unrepresented South or citizenship too fast); Congress overrode the veto.

keyIdeas: Mississippi’s laws of November 1865, passed by a government formed under Johnson’s plan, let Black people own personal property, sue and marry. They also restricted where and for whom Black people worked, how their children were raised and whether they could own weapons.

Under Mississippi’s vagrancy provision, Black adults without lawful employment or business could be fined, and those who could not pay could be hired out. Its apprenticeship provision let officials bind Black minors to employers when their parents were judged unable or unwilling to support them, even when both parents were alive. Employers who were former owners got preference.

Many Northerners read the Black Codes as slavery returning under new names. They were angry that the South was passing such laws months after Union victory, and that Georgia’s legislature had chosen Alexander Stephens in 1866, the former Confederate vice president, for the Senate.

The Civil Rights Act of 1866 declared people born in the United States citizens and listed equal rights, including making contracts, giving evidence and holding property. Johnson vetoed it on March 27, 1866, arguing that it intruded on state authority, that the Southern states had no voice in Congress, and that it gave citizenship to freed people too quickly. Congress overrode the veto in April.

A person with full legal membership in a nation, with rights the government must protect.

The president’s refusal to sign a bill into law.
A vote by two-thirds of both houses of Congress that makes a bill law despite a veto.

study.overview: After the Civil War, Southern governments formed under Johnson’s plan passed laws called the Black Codes. Mississippi’s laws of November 1865 gave Black people a few rights but placed heavy limits on work, family life and weapons. Many Northerners were angry, and Congress answered with the Civil Rights Act of 1866. Johnson vetoed it, and Congress overrode the veto. Use this guide to review what the laws did, why the North reacted and how the conflict was settled for the moment.

points.heading: What Mississippi’s 1865 laws allowed and restricted
points.explanation: Mississippi’s laws let Black people own personal property, sue in court and marry legally. But they also restricted where and for whom Black people worked, how their children were raised and whether they could own weapons. One example is the rule that Black adults had to show a lawful home or employment, with written proof each year. Another is the rule that Black people could not keep or carry firearms or bowie knives without a license. The laws named Black people and imposed racial restrictions. They did not say the word “slavery”, but the limits were written for one group of people.

points.heading: Vagrancy and apprenticeship: forced labor under the law
points.explanation: Two provisions show how the codes controlled labor. Under the vagrancy provision, Black adults with no lawful employment or business could be fined. If they could not pay, they could be hired out. This is the 13th Amendment’s exception clause in use, because the clause allows involuntary servitude as punishment for a crime. The apprenticeship provision let officials bind Black minors to an employer when their parents were judged unable or unwilling to support them. This could happen even when both parents were alive. Employers who were former owners got preference. Note that having no papers did not automatically make an adult a vagrant under the law. The provision applied to those without lawful employment or business.

points.heading: Why many Northerners were angry
points.explanation: Many Northerners read the Black Codes as slavery returning under new names. They were angry that the South was passing such laws only months after Union victory. They were also angry that Georgia’s legislature chose Alexander Stephens, the former Confederate vice president, for the Senate in 1866. Congress refused to seat Southern members. When you explain this reaction, name specific laws or officials, as in the examples above. Do not make claims about all Southerners.

points.heading: The Civil Rights Act of 1866, the veto and the override
points.explanation: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 declared people born in the United States citizens. It listed equal rights, including making contracts, giving evidence and holding property. Its guarantee of the right to make and enforce contracts challenges the home-or-employment rule. Its guarantee of full and equal benefit of the laws for the security of person and property challenges the firearms ban. Its guarantee of equal punishment challenges fines and hiring out. Apprenticeship is not clearly addressed. Johnson vetoed the act on March 27, 1866. He argued that it intruded on state authority, that the Southern states had no voice in Congress, and that it gave citizenship to freed people too quickly. Congress overrode the veto in April 1866, the Senate on April 6 and the House on April 9. This suggests that Congress, not the president, was now controlling Reconstruction. A law can still be repealed or ignored, so the question of enforcement stayed open.

l_d2fd67fd95aa.title: The 14th Amendment and Radical Reconstruction
l_d2fd67fd95aa.summary: Students study the 14th Amendment, the 1867 Reconstruction Acts and Johnson's impeachment, reading amendment text and a congressional speech; an exit ticket closes the class, and a short step toward the essay is set.

segments.title: Can a law be undone?
segments.description:
Return to the board questions about who controls Reconstruction and what rights freed people would have.
Display the Civil Rights Act’s guarantee of citizenship from last time. Ask what could stop a later Congress or a Southern state from weakening it.
Students write two sentences, then two students read aloud.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: Congress can repeal a law through the legislative process, and officials may fail to enforce it. A constitutional amendment is much harder to change, but it also needs enforcement. Last time the class named enforcement as a gap. Tell students today’s amendment is Congress’s answer. Ask about institutions, not individuals.

segments.title: Citizenship and equal protection
segments.description:
Explain that Congress passed the 14th Amendment in June 1866 and that it was ratified in July 1868.
Display Section 1 and read it aloud once. Students underline the citizenship clause (“All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens”) and the equal protection clause (“nor deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws”).
Students paraphrase each clause in one sentence. Note that Section 1 put the Civil Rights Act’s citizenship into the Constitution and reversed Dred Scott (1857), and that Section 3 barred many former Confederate officials from office.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: thinking it gave Black men the vote. It did not. The Reconstruction Acts required Black male voting in the affected states; next time, students examine the constitutional ban on denying voting rights because of race. Expected paraphrases: people born or naturalized in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens; a state must treat people equally under its laws. Johnson urged Southern states to reject it; Tennessee was the only one to ratify in 1866.

segments.title: Testing the clauses against Mississippi’s laws
segments.description:
Pairs get four cases on a half sheet, each based on a restriction from the Mississippi laws studied last time.
For each case, they decide whether the citizenship clause, the equal protection clause or both apply, and write one sentence of reasoning.
Pairs share their answer to the last case with the class.
segments.teacherNotes:
Cases, with expected answers, one per line:
1. A Black adult with no lawful employment or business is fined for vagrancy and, unable to pay, is hired out. Equal protection: the law punishes by race.
2. Officials bind a Black child to a former owner after judging the child’s living parents unable or unwilling to provide support. Equal protection: this provision specifically targets Black children and gives former owners preference.
3. A county clerk says a Black man born in Mississippi is not a citizen. Citizenship clause: birth makes him a citizen.
4. A state bans only Black residents from owning weapons. Equal protection.
Accept both clauses where argued. Name restrictions as the laws wrote them.

segments.title: Military districts and the clash with Johnson
segments.description:
Explain that Congress passed the first Reconstruction Act on March 2, 1867, over Johnson’s veto. Ten Southern states were placed in five military districts, each under an army commander. Tennessee was left out because it had already ratified the 14th Amendment.
Students label a blank map of the South with the five districts as you name them.
Explain what each state had to do to rejoin the Union: write a new constitution that let Black men vote, and ratify the 14th Amendment.
Close with Johnson’s removal of Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in February 1868, the House vote to impeach him and the Senate’s acquittal by one vote in May 1868.
segments.teacherNotes:
Prepare a blank map of the South. Districts, one per line:
1. Virginia
2. North Carolina and South Carolina
3. Georgia, Alabama and Florida
4. Mississippi and Arkansas
5. Louisiana and Texas
Explain that the House charged Johnson with violating the Tenure of Office Act by removing Stanton without Senate approval. Johnson’s defense disputed whether the law applied to Stanton. Common mistake: impeachment means removal. Johnson stayed in office.

segments.title: Reading Thaddeus Stevens
segments.description:
Hand out the passage from Thaddeus Stevens’s speech to the House of Representatives of December 18, 1865. Read it aloud once. Name Stevens as a Radical Republican who wanted Congress to set the terms for the South.
Students read silently and underline what Stevens says Congress should decide before the Southern states return.
Pairs answer the two questions on the board in complete sentences.
segments.teacherNotes:
Prepare copies of Thaddeus Stevens, speech to the House of Representatives, December 18, 1865, the passage that begins “The future condition of the conquered power” and ends “the only power that can act in the matter”. Questions and expected answers:
1. Who does Stevens say should decide the terms for the South? Congress, not the president acting alone.
2. Why does he want Congress to decide? Because he treats the South as conquered land.
Stevens is one side of a dispute, not a neutral witness. Tell students the speech was given fifteen months before the first Reconstruction Act.

segments.title: Why did Congress take control?
segments.description:
Pose the question: why did Congress take control of Reconstruction from Johnson?
On the board, list four pieces of evidence: the Black Codes, the override of the Civil Rights Act, Johnson’s opposition to the 14th Amendment and Stevens’s argument.
Each student picks the strongest reason and explains it to a partner. Then the class votes by show of hands and two students defend their choices.
segments.teacherNotes: Accept any choice backed by evidence. Strong answers link the Black Codes to Congress’s belief that Johnson’s plan left freed people unprotected. Others cite the override as proof Congress had the votes. Redirect generalizations about all Southerners to the laws and legislatures.

segments.title: Exit ticket
segments.description:
Students answer on a half sheet and hand it in.
Question: Explain how the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment challenges one restriction in Mississippi’s 1865 laws. Name one thing the Reconstruction Acts required of Southern states. Then give one reason Congress took control of Reconstruction from Johnson.
Collect before the bell.

Score it 0–3: 3 for every part correct, 2 for most parts correct, 1 for an attempt with a major gap, 0 if not handed in. Expected: a restriction applied only to Black people, such as the vagrancy fine or the weapons ban, which the clause bars states from enforcing; a requirement (new constitution with Black men voting, or ratifying the 14th Amendment); a reason (Black Codes, veto override, or Johnson’s opposition).

segments.title: Setting the essay step
segments.description:
Before students leave, hand out the take-home sheet for the short ungraded step toward the document-based essay.
Tell them it prepares them for that essay, which counts for 50% of the course grade.
Tell them to bring the finished sheet next time.
segments.teacherNotes: Prepare copies of the sheet before class. Say that it is ungraded and starts the evidence bank they will use for the essay. Give out the sheet at the door so exit tickets are collected first.

keyIdeas: The 14th Amendment, passed by Congress in June 1866 and ratified in July 1868, wrote citizenship for people born in the United States into the Constitution. Its equal protection clause barred any state from denying ‘the equal protection of the laws’ to any person.

The Reconstruction Acts of March 1867 divided ten Southern states into five military districts under army commanders. To rejoin the Union, each state had to write a new constitution that let Black men vote and had to ratify the 14th Amendment.

Congress passed the Reconstruction Acts over Johnson’s vetoes. Radical Republicans such as Thaddeus Stevens argued that Congress, not the president, had the power to decide the terms for readmitting the Southern states.

Johnson clashed with Congress over the Tenure of Office Act and his removal of Secretary of War Edwin Stanton. The House impeached him in February 1868, and the Senate acquitted him in May 1868 by one vote.

vocabulary.definition: Members of Congress, such as Thaddeus Stevens, who wanted Congress to set strict terms for the South and to protect the rights of freed people.
The 14th Amendment’s rule that no state may deny any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.
The rule that a state may not take a person’s life, liberty or property without fair legal procedures.
Laws passed by Congress in 1867 that placed ten Southern states under army rule until they wrote new constitutions and ratified the 14th Amendment.
One of the five Southern regions under an army commander, set up by the Reconstruction Acts.
An 1867 law that stopped the president from removing certain officials, such as the Secretary of War, without the Senate’s approval.
To charge a public official with wrongdoing in office. In the federal government the House brings the charges and the Senate holds the trial.
To find a person not guilty. The Senate acquitted Johnson in 1868 because it fell one vote short of the two-thirds needed to convict.

study.overview: Last time, you saw that laws like the Civil Rights Act could be weakened by a later Congress or ignored by Southern officials. The 14th Amendment was Congress’s answer: it put citizenship and equal treatment into the Constitution. When Southern states resisted, Congress passed the Reconstruction Acts of 1867 and took control of Reconstruction from President Andrew Johnson. This guide reviews the amendment, the military districts, and why Congress and Johnson clashed. Use it to prepare for the short take-home step toward your document-based essay.

points.heading: Citizenship and equal protection in the 14th Amendment
points.explanation: Congress passed the 14th Amendment in June 1866, and it was ratified in July 1868. Section 1 has two key clauses. The citizenship clause says that ‘All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens.’ This put the citizenship of the Civil Rights Act into the Constitution and reversed Dred Scott (1857). The equal protection clause says no state may ‘deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.’ Example: a Mississippi law under the Black Codes fined a Black adult for vagrancy if he had no lawful employment or business, and hired him out if he could not pay. The law punished people by race, so the equal protection clause challenges it. A county clerk who said a Black man born in Mississippi was not a citizen would be challenged by the citizenship clause, because birth makes him a citizen. Do not confuse the amendment with voting. It did not give Black men the vote. Section 3 also barred many former Confederate officials from office.

points.heading: The Reconstruction Acts and the military districts
points.explanation: On March 2, 1867, Congress passed the first Reconstruction Act over Johnson’s veto. It placed ten Southern states in five military districts, each under an army commander. Tennessee was left out because it had already ratified the 14th Amendment. The districts were: Virginia; North Carolina and South Carolina; Georgia, Alabama and Florida; Mississippi and Arkansas; and Louisiana and Texas. To rejoin the Union, each state had to write a new constitution that let Black men vote, and each had to ratify the 14th Amendment. Example: Louisiana and Texas shared one district. To be readmitted, both had to hold constitutional conventions that included Black voters and then approve the amendment. Johnson had urged Southern states to reject the amendment, and Tennessee was the only one to ratify in 1866.

points.heading: Why Congress took control from Johnson
points.explanation: Several pieces of evidence help explain why Congress took control. The Black Codes suggested that Johnson’s plan left freed people unprotected. Congress overrode his veto of the Civil Rights Act, which showed it had the votes. Johnson also opposed the 14th Amendment. Radical Republicans such as Thaddeus Stevens argued that Congress, not the president, should decide the terms for readmitting the Southern states. In his speech to the House of Representatives on December 18, 1865, Stevens treated the South as conquered land, which is why he said Congress should set the terms. Remember that Stevens was one side of a dispute, not a neutral witness. When you use him in writing, say whose view it is. Example of a strong argument: the Black Codes convinced many in Congress that the president’s plan was not protecting freed people, so Congress acted. Make your claim about the laws and legislatures, not about all Southerners.

points.heading: Johnson’s impeachment
points.explanation: The conflict between Johnson and Congress reached a peak over the Tenure of Office Act. In February 1868, Johnson removed Secretary of War Edwin Stanton. The House charged him with violating the act by removing Stanton without Senate approval. Johnson’s defense disputed whether the law applied to Stanton. The House impeached him in February 1868, and the Senate acquitted him in May 1868 by one vote. Common mistake: impeachment does not mean removal. It is the House’s formal charge, like an indictment. Johnson was impeached but stayed in office because the Senate did not convict.

segments.title: Writing a voting amendment
segments.description:
Take in the essay sheet from last time at the door and check that it is done.
Post the board questions from earlier in the course about who controls Reconstruction and what rights freed people would have.
Remind the class that the Reconstruction Acts made Black men voters in ten Southern states, but the 14th Amendment gave no one the vote.
Students write one sentence for an amendment that protects Black men’s vote, then one way someone could get around it. Two students read aloud.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: ban denying the vote because of race; evasions include new tests, taxes or biased officials. The sheet is ungraded, so check only that it is done and return it. Do not reveal the 15th Amendment’s wording yet.

segments.title: What the 15th Amendment says
segments.description:
Explain that many Northern states still limited Black voting in 1869, so Congress wrote a national rule.
Congress passed the 15th Amendment in February 1869 and the states ratified it in 1870.
Display Section 1 and read it aloud once.
Students underline the three reasons a state may not use to deny the vote.
segments.teacherNotes: Section 1: “The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” Section 2: “Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation.” Expected underlines: race, color, previous condition of servitude. Common mistake: reading it as “all citizens may vote.” Prepare copies of both sections.

segments.title: Guaranteed or left out?
segments.description:
Pairs get six statements on a half sheet. For each, they mark Guaranteed, Left out or Needs enforcement, and write a reason in a few words.
Ask who must act when a rule’s wording is neutral but the way it is used is not.
Show Section 2 and note that enforcement was left to Congress.
Pairs revise one answer and share it.
segments.teacherNotes:
Statements with answers:
1. A state bars men from voting because they were enslaved before 1865. Guaranteed: “previous condition of servitude” is named.
2. A state constitution says only white men may vote. Guaranteed: race is named, so it is barred on its face.
3. A state gives the vote to men only. Left out: the amendment does not name sex.
4. A hypothetical state makes every voter pay a $2 yearly tax, worded the same for all. Left out: neutral wording is not clearly banned, yet the tax can shut out poor freed people.
5. A hypothetical county registrar gives Black applicants a hard reading test and lets white applicants pass an easy one, under a test law that applies to everyone on paper. Needs enforcement: the wording is neutral but the unequal tests discriminate because of race and violate the amendment. Enforcement is needed to stop the violation.
6. A state refuses to let a Black man who won an election take office. Left out: the amendment protects voting, not officeholding.
Mistakes: neutral wording means fair; neutral wording means legal.

segments.title: Black political life in the South
segments.description:
Explain that Black men voted in the 1867 and 1868 elections and helped write new state constitutions. In South Carolina, a majority of the delegates were Black.
Introduce Hiram Revels, who was elected to the Senate by the Mississippi legislature in January 1870, a few weeks before the 15th Amendment was ratified.
Pairs read the Article X excerpt and the Revels fact card. For each source they note what changed and who made it happen.
segments.teacherNotes:
Prepare copies of two sections of Article X (Education) of the South Carolina Constitution of 1868: Section 3, which tells the legislature to set up a uniform system of free public schools across the state, and Section 10, which opens public schools and colleges to all children without regard to race or color.
Expected notes: Article X made free public schools a duty of the state, written by a convention with a Black majority. The fact card shows a Black man seated in the Senate, chosen by Mississippi’s legislature.
Fact card, to prepare:
- Hiram Revels, born free in North Carolina in 1827, was a minister and Union Army chaplain.
- In January 1870 the Mississippi legislature elected him to the Senate, to a seat once held by Albert G. Brown.
- Some senators argued he had not been a citizen long enough. The Senate voted 48 to 8 to seat him on February 25, 1870.
- He was the first Black person to sit in Congress.
- Blanche K. Bruce of Mississippi served in the Senate from 1875 to 1881.
Revels was elected before the 15th Amendment was ratified on February 3, 1870. Black men in Mississippi already voted under the Reconstruction Acts, so do not present his election as a result of the amendment.
The seating debate included racist arguments. Summarize them and quote none aloud; students do not speak as any senator.

segments.title: Build a claim from two sources
segments.description:
Model the steps with an everyday case first. Suppose a school handbook and a club poster both show that a school values student voice.
Pairs choose two of the three sources: Section 1 of the 15th Amendment, the Article X excerpt and the Revels fact card.
They write one claim about Reconstruction’s achievements, then a short paragraph that names both sources and says what each one shows.
segments.teacherNotes: Frame: “Reconstruction opened public life to Black Southerners because ___ (Source) and ___ (Source).” Any two sources fit this claim: amendment plus Article X, amendment plus fact card, or Article X plus fact card. Strong paragraphs say “opened,” not “ensured.” Ungraded practice for the essay skill.

segments.title: What can the sources prove?
segments.description:
Three pairs read their claims aloud.
The class says what each source proves and what it cannot show.
Ask what separates a law on paper from what happened in practice, and who had to enforce the law.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: the amendment shows a rule, Article X shows a plan, the fact card shows one person’s success. None shows how many Black men actually voted or went to school. Link to the sorting: enforcement is the open question. Next time the class examines violence against voters.

segments.title: Exit ticket
segments.description:
Students answer on a half sheet and hand it in.
Question: Name one thing the 15th Amendment guaranteed and one thing it left out. Then describe one gain made by Black officeholders or the new Southern state governments.
Collect before the bell.
segments.teacherNotes: Counts toward the lesson exit tickets component (30% of the course grade). Score out of 3, one point for each part. Expected: guaranteed that the vote could not be denied because of race, color or previous servitude. Left out: women, literacy tests, poll taxes, officeholding, or a positive right to vote. Gain: Revels in the Senate, Black delegates writing constitutions, or public schools.

segments.title: Setting the essay step
segments.description:
Before students leave, hand out the take-home sheet for the short ungraded step toward the document-based essay, with copies of the three sources from today.
Tell them it prepares them for that essay, which counts for 50% of the course grade.
Tell them to bring the finished sheet next time.
segments.teacherNotes: Prepare copies of the sheet and the three sources before class. The step is ungraded: students add today’s sources to their evidence bank and write a tentative answer to the essay question. Give it out at the door so exit tickets are collected first.

keyIdeas: The 15th Amendment, passed by Congress in February 1869 and ratified in 1870, barred the United States and any state from denying or abridging the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.”

The amendment left gaps. It gave no positive right to vote, did not cover women, did not mention officeholding, and did not ban literacy tests or poll taxes. A rule can be race-neutral in its wording and still be used to exclude Black voters. Section 2 left enforcement to Congress.

Black men voted in the Southern elections of 1867 and 1868 and helped write new state constitutions. Hundreds served in state legislatures. In 1870 Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black member of the U.S. Senate.

The new Southern state governments created public school systems. South Carolina’s 1868 constitution provided for free public schools, one example of what Black political participation helped bring about.
A strong claim about Reconstruction’s achievements joins two sources and says what each one shows. A law or plan on paper does not prove the result in practice.

study.overview: The 15th Amendment, passed by Congress in February 1869 and ratified in 1870, said that no state or the United States could deny or abridge the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It was a major step, but it had gaps. Black men also took part in Southern politics in new ways: they voted, helped write state constitutions and held office. The new Southern state governments built public school systems. When you write about Reconstruction’s achievements, remember that a law on paper does not prove what happened in practice.

points.heading: What the 15th Amendment guaranteed
points.explanation: Section 1 names three reasons that cannot be used to deny or abridge the vote: race, color and previous condition of servitude. Many Northern states still limited Black voting in 1869, so Congress wrote a national rule. Example: a state constitution that says only white men may vote is barred on its face, because race is named. So is a state that bars men from voting because they were enslaved before 1865. Be careful: the amendment does not say that all citizens may vote. It only limits the reasons a state may use.

points.heading: What the amendment left out
points.explanation: The amendment gave no positive right to vote. It did not cover women, did not mention officeholding, and did not ban literacy tests or poll taxes. A rule can be race-neutral in its wording and still shut out Black voters. Example: suppose a state makes every voter pay a $2 yearly tax, worded the same for all. The wording is neutral, yet the tax can shut out poor freed people. Another case: a registrar gives Black applicants a hard reading test and white applicants an easy one. The law applies to everyone on paper, but the unequal tests discriminate because of race and violate the amendment. Section 2 says, “Congress shall have power to enforce this article by appropriate legislation,” so enforcement was left to Congress. Neutral wording does not mean fair, and it does not mean legal.

points.heading: Black political life and the new state governments
points.explanation: Black men voted in the Southern elections of 1867 and 1868 and helped write new state constitutions. In South Carolina, a majority of the delegates were Black. Hundreds served in state legislatures. In 1870, the Mississippi legislature elected Hiram Revels, a minister and Union Army chaplain born free in North Carolina in 1827, to the U.S. Senate. The Senate voted 48 to 8 to seat him on February 25, 1870, and he became the first Black person to sit in Congress. The new state governments also created public school systems. South Carolina’s 1868 constitution provided for free public schools. These are examples of what Black political participation helped bring about.

points.heading: Building a strong claim from two sources
points.explanation: A strong claim joins two sources and says what each one shows. For example: “Reconstruction opened public life to Black Southerners because the 15th Amendment barred denying the vote on account of race (Source 1) and Hiram Revels was seated in the Senate (Source 2).” Notice the word “opened,” not “ensured.” The amendment shows a rule. Article X shows a plan. The Revels fact card shows one person’s success. None of them shows how many Black men actually voted or went to school. A law or plan on paper does not prove the result in practice, so ask who had to enforce it.

l_bec7edf76a44.title: The Ku Klux Klan and the Enforcement Acts
l_bec7edf76a44.summary: Students analyze Klan violence, testimony from the 1871 congressional investigation and the Enforcement Acts of 1870–1871; an exit ticket closes the class, and an essay step is set.

segments.title: Who enforces the amendment?
segments.description:
Collect the essay sheet from last time at the door and check that it is done. Display the question from last time: what separates a law on paper from what happened in practice, and who had to enforce the law?
Students write two sentences on this: the 15th Amendment bars denying the vote because of race, so what else could someone do to stop Black men from voting?
Two students read aloud, and you list their ideas on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: threats, beatings, burning homes, and officials who look away. Say that today’s lesson is about that gap. The sheet is ungraded: check only that it is done and return it. Revisit the board questions from earlier in the course on who controls Reconstruction and what rights freed people would have.

segments.title: Why the Klan formed and whom it targeted
segments.description:
Explain that six former Confederate soldiers founded the Klan in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1865–1866, first as a social club. It soon became a secret network that spread across the South, with members who wore disguises and rode at night.
Name who was targeted: Black voters and officeholders, white Republicans, Freedmen’s Bureau agents, teachers of freed people, and Black families who owned land or refused low-wage labor terms.
Students fill a three-row note chart: Who was targeted, What the Klan wanted to stop, Why it mattered to white Democrats who led it.
Tie the targets back to the 14th and 15th Amendments and the new Southern governments.
segments.teacherNotes: Content note: say plainly that this lesson covers real violence and that the class studies it as history. Use the term Klansmen for the attackers and never assign students to play victims or perpetrators. Expected chart: power over voting, labor and schools. Avoid saying all white Southerners joined the Klan; many did not.

segments.title: Matching targets to goals
segments.description:
Pairs get five short cases on a half sheet. The cases are invented, but each follows a pattern historians have documented.
For each case, pairs name the target and mark the Klan’s goal: Voting and office, Labor and land, or Schools and equal status.
Pairs share their answer to the last case, then write one sentence on what the five cases share.
segments.teacherNotes:
Cases with answers, one per line:
1. Suppose a Black man in a Mississippi county is warned the night before an election not to vote Republican. Target: Black voter. Goal: Voting and office.
2. Suppose a white Republican sheriff in North Carolina is ordered to resign. Target: white Republican officeholder. Goal: Voting and office.
3. Suppose a Black tenant in Georgia refuses a low-wage contract and his barn is burned. Target: Black farmer. Goal: Labor and land.
4. Suppose a Northern-born teacher at a freedpeople’s school in Alabama gets a note ordering her to leave. Target: teacher. Goal: Schools and equal status.
5. Suppose a Black couple in Louisiana who bought land are told to sell and leave. Target: Black landowners. Goal: Labor and land.
Shared: violence aimed to keep Black Southerners from independence and power.

segments.title: Two witnesses before Congress
segments.description:
Explain that Congress set up a joint committee in 1871 to investigate the Klan and heard testimony in Washington and across the South. Hand out two short excerpts and say who each witness is: Elias Hill, a Black Baptist minister and teacher from York County, South Carolina, and Nathan Bedford Forrest, a former Confederate general.
Pairs read both silently and complete a chart with one row per witness: who is speaking, what the witness claims, point of view, and purpose.
Pairs write one sentence on why Congress might trust or question each account.
Take two pairs’ answers.
segments.teacherNotes:
Prepare copies from the testimony the committee took in 1871, printed in 1872 with the Report of the Joint Select Committee to Inquire into the Condition of Affairs in the Late Insurrectionary States: (1) Elias Hill, testimony at Yorkville, South Carolina, July 25, 1871, the passage where he describes the night of May 5, 1871, when Klansmen came to his house; (2) Nathan Bedford Forrest, testimony in Washington, June 27, 1871, the passage where he is asked whether he belonged to the Klan. Trim each to a short passage.
Expected: Hill, who could not walk, was carried into his yard and beaten. He was a victim who risked retaliation and wanted Congress to act. Forrest denied membership and downplayed the group to protect himself and the South from federal action. Historians widely identify Forrest as a Klan leader.
Content note: Hill’s account describes a beating. Warn students before they read, and remind them that anyone may step out for a moment without asking. If any part is read aloud, slurs are skipped, not spoken.

segments.title: The Enforcement Acts
segments.description:
Explain that Congress passed three laws in 1870–1871. The first (May 1870) made it a federal crime to use force or threats to stop citizens from voting. The second (February 1871) allowed federal supervision of elections in large cities. The third, the Ku Klux Klan Act (April 1871), made conspiracies to deprive people of their rights a federal crime and let the president use the army.
In October 1871, President Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties, and federal prosecutors tried many Klansmen.
Students make a separate chart with one row for each act and two columns: the act and the tool it gave the government.
segments.teacherNotes: The Justice Department was created in 1870; Attorney General Amos Akerman led the prosecutions. Habeas corpus is the right to challenge imprisonment before a judge. Explain that earlier reports of violence helped prompt the laws. Hill’s and Forrest’s testimony came after all three acts had passed and helped Congress investigate the violence and the need for enforcement.

segments.title: How effective were the Enforcement Acts?
segments.description:
Give the evidence: the Klan was broken in many places by 1872, but groups such as the White League and Red Shirts used violence openly in the years after. In 1876 the Supreme Court in United States v. Cruikshank limited the government’s power to prosecute private attackers.
Students write one sentence rating the acts as effective, partly effective or ineffective, and name one piece of evidence.

points.heading: Why the Klan formed and whom it targeted
points.explanation: The Klan started as a social club and soon became a secret network whose members wore disguises and rode at night. Klansmen targeted Black voters and officeholders, white Republicans, Freedmen’s Bureau agents, teachers of freed people, and Black families who owned land or refused low-wage labor terms. Their goals fell into three groups: voting and office, labor and land, and schools and equal status. Example: suppose a Black tenant in Georgia refuses a low-wage contract and his barn is burned. The target is a Black farmer and the goal is labor and land. Across all such cases, violence aimed to keep Black Southerners from independence and power.

points.heading: Judging witness accounts as evidence
points.explanation: A historian asks three questions of any account: who is speaking, what did that person risk or hope to gain, and who was the audience? In 1871 a joint committee of Congress took testimony from victims and from Southern leaders. Elias Hill, a Black Baptist minister from York County, South Carolina, described the night Klansmen came to his house. He was a victim who risked retaliation, and he wanted Congress to act. Nathan Bedford Forrest, a former Confederate general, was asked whether he belonged to the Klan and denied it. He wanted to protect himself and the South from federal action, and historians widely identify him as a Klan leader. Each account is useful, but a reader must weigh point of view and purpose before trusting it.

points.heading: The Enforcement Acts and how well they worked

The February 1871 act allowed federal supervision of elections in large cities. The Ku Klux Klan Act of April 1871 made conspiracies to deprive people of their rights a federal crime and let the president use the army. In October 1871, President Grant suspended habeas corpus, the right to challenge imprisonment before a judge, in nine South Carolina counties, and federal prosecutors tried many Klansmen. Cruikshank limited the government’s power to prosecute private attackers. l_afe3711f5c21.summary: Students hold the graded Socratic seminar on whether Reconstruction failed, citing documents from earlier classes; afterward the document-based essay is set.

segments.title: Rules, rubric and a model move
segments.description:
Collect the Hayes inaugural address sheets from last time at the door and check that they are done.
Display the four seminar levels: Excellent, Good, Developing and Beginning. Tell students the seminar is graded and counts for 20% of the course grade.
Model one move on a different question: “Should our school start an hour later?” Say a claim, then answer it with counterevidence: “Suppose a survey of our school found that most students sleep under eight hours. That supports a later start. Suppose a district transportation report also found that a later start would leave students without bus service. That evidence weighs against changing the start time.”
Students name which part was the claim, the evidence and the counterevidence.
segments.teacherNotes: Sheet is ungraded: check it is done and return it. Levels, scored only on what a student says in the circle. Excellent: names a document, says what it shows, and answers a classmate with specific evidence. Good: names a document and says what it shows, but answers classmates in general terms or not at all. Developing: opinion, no document named. Beginning: does not speak, even when invited. One turn of about 30 seconds can earn Excellent. Students answer as themselves, never as historical people.

segments.title: Ready the position card
segments.description:
Students take out last time’s position card, their evidence bank and their document copies.
They circle the two documents named on the card and write beside each the claim it supports.
They add one counterargument a classmate might raise and the document that answers it.
Split the class into two circles, A and B.
segments.teacherNotes: Walk the room and check each student has two named documents, not just a general claim. Documents students can name include the 14th or 15th Amendment, the Mississippi Black Code of 1865, Article X of South Carolina’s 1868 constitution, Elias Hill’s testimony and Hayes’s inaugural address. Students who have no second document take one from the evidence bank. Split the class evenly and pair each student with a partner in the other circle to track.

segments.title: Seminar round one: circle A speaks
segments.description:
Circle A sits in the inner ring and circle B sits outside with a tracking sheet.
Open with the question: “Did Reconstruction fail?”
Inner-ring students speak to each other, cite a document by name for each claim, and answer the previous speaker with specific counterevidence.
Each outer-ring student tracks one partner in the inner ring: a tally mark each time the partner names a document and each time the partner answers a classmate with evidence. They also note one question to ask in round two.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep a class list with two columns: D for naming a document and saying what it shows, R for answering a classmate with specific evidence. Tick as students speak and do not comment aloud. After class, D and R make Excellent, D alone Good, speaking with no tick Developing, silence Beginning; the partners’ tracking sheets back up your ticks. With about 14 students in the circle each has under a minute, so ask for turns of about 30 seconds, and in the last three minutes call on anyone who has not spoken. Prompts if talk stalls: What does “failed” mean, compared with which goal? Which document shows that? What does that document leave out? Handle violence in sources factually. Slurs are not said aloud, anyone may step out for a moment without asking, and no one role-plays victims or perpetrators.

segments.title: Seminar round two: circle B speaks
segments.description:
The circles swap places, and circle B now holds the inner ring.
Begin by asking circle B to respond to one claim from round one with counterevidence.
Students build on what circle A said, concede points they find convincing, and cite documents by name.
The outer ring tallies as before and tells the inner ring one strong move they heard.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep ticking the same two columns, and collect the tracking sheets when the round ends. Invite quiet students in with a direct question about a document they chose. Expected positions: failed because troops left and Black voting was suppressed; did not fail because the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments remained; or a qualified middle view.

segments.title: Exit ticket: revise your thesis
segments.description:
Students write on a half sheet and hand it in. The question has two parts.
First: Write your revised thesis on whether Reconstruction failed, in one or two sentences, and name two documents you could use to support it.
Second: Name one piece of counterevidence a classmate raised in the seminar and say how it changed or kept your thesis.
Students copy the thesis onto their position card so they keep it for the essay. Collect the half sheets before the bell.
segments.teacherNotes: Counts toward the lesson exit tickets component (30% of the course grade). Score out of 3: a thesis that takes a position (1), two documents named (1), a classmate’s point addressed (1). Expected: a thesis with a clear claim and a qualification, e.g. Reconstruction failed to protect Black Southerners’ rights by 1877 because troops left and Redeemers took over, though the amendments remained; two named documents; one specific classmate point addressed.

segments.title: Set the essay assignment
segments.description:
Before students leave, hand out the document-based essay assignment sheet and the packet of documents.
Tell students the essay is 50% of the course grade and is due at the start of class one week from today, on paper or through the class site. Write the date on the board.
Tell them to read the sheet tonight and bring questions to the next class.
Thank the class for a respectful seminar.
segments.teacherNotes: Prepare copies of the assignment sheet, the rubric and the document packet before class. The packet holds a clean copy of every document listed on the sheet. Give them out after the exit tickets are collected. Remind students that late essays lose 5% a day.

keyIdeas: Whether Reconstruction failed depends on the standard used. Measured against its goals of citizenship, equal rights and Black political power, the outcome was weaker than the promise.

The evidence points both ways. The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments stayed in the Constitution, and Black men voted and held office. Federal troops left in 1877, Redeemer Democrats controlled every Southern state, and Black Southerners lost most federal protection.
A strong historical argument names a specific document and answers a classmate’s counterevidence instead of repeating a claim.
Good historians concede what the other side gets right, then qualify their thesis. The thesis for the document-based essay gets sharper through discussion.

vocabulary.definition: A structured group discussion in which students question and answer each other about a text or problem, using evidence.
Evidence that goes against a claim or weakens it.
The central argument of an essay, stated in one or two sentences and supported by evidence.
To admit that part of an opposing argument is correct before explaining your own view.
