study.overview: In this seminar you argued about whether Reconstruction failed. There is no single right answer. The answer depends on the standard you use and on the documents you cite. This guide reviews how to build that kind of argument and how to sharpen your thesis for the document-based essay.

points.heading: The answer depends on your standard
points.explanation: To say Reconstruction failed, you first have to say what it was supposed to do. Its goals were citizenship, equal rights and Black political power. Measured against those goals, the outcome was weaker than the promise. Measured against a lower standard, such as keeping the Union together, you might reach a different answer. Example: if you say Reconstruction failed, name the goal you are using. You might write, “Compared with the goal of equal rights, it fell short by 1877.” That tells your reader how to judge your claim.

points.heading: The evidence points both ways
points.explanation: Some evidence supports the view that Reconstruction failed. Federal troops left in 1877. Redeemer Democrats controlled every Southern state. Black Southerners lost most federal protection. Other evidence supports the view that it did not fail. The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments stayed in the Constitution, and Black men voted and held office. Example: Elias Hill’s testimony could be used for the first view, because it shows the violence that kept Black Southerners from using their rights. The text of the amendments could be used for the second view, because it shows rights that stayed in the law. A strong essay uses both kinds of evidence.

points.heading: Name the document and answer the counterevidence
points.explanation: A strong argument does more than repeat a claim. It names a specific document for each claim. It also answers a classmate’s counterevidence with specifics. Compare two moves. Weak: “Reconstruction failed because things got worse.” Stronger: “Reconstruction failed to protect Black Southerners’ rights by 1877. Elias Hill’s testimony shows Klansmen beating a Black minister in 1871, and Hayes’s inaugural address shows a president promising the South local self-government.” The second version names documents and gives the reader something to check. Practice the same move on any topic. Claim: a later school start helps students. Evidence: a survey finding most students sleep under eight hours. Counterevidence: a transportation report finding a later start would leave students without bus service.

points.heading: Concede, then qualify your thesis
points.explanation: Good historians admit what the other side gets right. Then they adjust their claim to fit. This makes a thesis sharper, not weaker. Example: a first thesis might say, “Reconstruction failed.” After hearing a classmate point to the amendments, you might revise it: “Reconstruction failed to protect Black Southerners’ rights by 1877 because troops left and Redeemers took over, though the amendments remained.” This version has a clear claim and a qualification. Use this model, with your own position and your own two documents, as you work on the thesis for your document-based essay.

t_96811a45d3ba.prompt: Lincoln’s plan needed only 10 percent of a state’s 1860 voters to take a loyalty oath. Johnson’s plan pardoned most Southerners who swore an oath, but made wealthy Confederates apply to him personally. Which approach was the better way to bring the South back into the Union in 1865? Take a position and give a reason from the plans.
followUps: Both plans were made by the president alone, without Congress. What are the risks and the benefits of one person deciding the terms?
Johnson granted thousands of individual pardons, and planters regained political power fast. Does that change your answer? Why or why not?
The 1860 voters were white men only. Who did that leave out, and should their voices have counted in forming new state governments?

t_c3d06606021b.prompt: In the Second Inaugural, Lincoln asks the nation to act ‘with malice toward none’ and to bind up the nation’s wounds. In 1865, was it more important to be generous toward former Confederates or to protect the freed people? Can a country do both? Defend your view.
followUps: Neither plan gave Black men the vote, citizenship or land. What did freedom mean for formerly enslaved people without those things?
Which of the four questions of 1865 (who controls Reconstruction, terms for readmission, who is pardoned or punished, rights of freed people) would you settle first, and why?
What in Lincoln’s words suggests his priorities, and what do the excerpts leave unsaid?

t_89f780bc31e6.prompt: Under Lincoln’s Ten Percent Plan, when could a Confederate state form a new government?

choices.text: When 10 percent of its current residents swore loyalty and accepted the end of slavery
When 10 percent of its 1860 voters swore loyalty and accepted the end of slavery
When a majority of its 1860 voters swore loyalty under a stricter oath
When a majority of its current voters swore loyalty and accepted the end of slavery

t_89f780bc31e6.explanation: Lincoln’s plan used 10 percent of a state’s 1860 voters, not its current population. Those voters had to swear loyalty and accept emancipation.

t_db423709ccee.prompt: In the paragraph of his Second Inaugural that begins “One-eighth of the whole population were colored slaves,” what did Lincoln identify as the war’s cause?

choices.text: Disputes over state governments were the cause of the war
The Union’s wartime taxes were the cause of the war
Slavery was a powerful interest known to be the cause of the war
Confederate debt was the cause of the war

t_db423709ccee.explanation: Lincoln says the slaves “constituted a peculiar and powerful interest” and that all knew this interest “was somehow the cause of the war.”

t_94f7b12890dd.prompt: In summer 1865, a former Confederate official with $24,000 in taxable property swears Johnson’s loyalty oath. What else did he need for a pardon under Johnson’s plan?

choices.text: He had to apply personally to Johnson for a pardon
He had to wait for 10 percent of 1860 voters to swear loyalty
He had to apply to Congress for a pardon
He had to wait for a majority of 1860 voters to swear loyalty

t_94f7b12890dd.explanation: Under Johnson’s plan, Confederate officials and people with more than $20,000 in taxable property had to apply to him personally.

t_3d99da607418.prompt: In the final paragraph of his Second Inaugural, Lincoln called for malice toward none and a lasting peace.

choices.text: True
False

t_3d99da607418.explanation: Lincoln’s closing appeal called for no malice, healing the nation’s wounds, and a lasting peace.

t_f414b6054049.prompt: Name two questions about Reconstruction that neither Lincoln’s nor Johnson’s plan settled.
t_f414b6054049.answer: Who would control Reconstruction, and what rights formerly enslaved people would have beyond freedom from slavery, such as citizenship, voting rights, or land.
t_f414b6054049.explanation: Both plans were made by the president without Congress, and neither settled the rights of freed people.

t_21a5357c5e5f.prompt: The Mississippi laws of November 1865 gave Black people some rights: to own personal property, to sue in court and to marry legally. They also restricted where and for whom Black people worked, how their children were raised and whether they could keep weapons. Some Mississippi officials might have said the laws were a reasonable way to keep order after the war. Was the state granting rights, or was it controlling people? Use the laws we sorted to decide, and say which restriction is your strongest evidence.
followUps: Which of the laws we sorted would you point to first if you were arguing that the Black Codes were slavery under new names? Which would a defender of the laws point to? Does it matter that the laws named Black people and listed specific restrictions?
The laws let Black people sue and marry. Does granting some rights change your answer about the restrictions, or can a law give rights and take them away at once?

Many Northerners were angry that the laws came months after Union victory. Which parts of the laws help explain that anger, and which would you cite to show that the laws were passed under Johnson’s plan?

t_8d67feeab83d.prompt: Johnson vetoed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 on March 27, 1866. He argued that it intruded on state authority, that the Southern states had no voice in Congress, and that it gave citizenship to freed people too quickly. Congress overrode the veto in April. Which of Johnson’s three arguments was the strongest, and was it strong enough to outweigh the guarantees in Section 1 in light of the Mississippi laws? Take a position and use a specific law and a specific guarantee as evidence.
followUps: Johnson’s second argument was that Southern states had no representatives in Congress. Is that a fair objection to the law, or does the Mississippi legislation weaken it? Think about Georgia’s choice of Alexander Stephens as well.

Section 1 listed rights such as making contracts, giving evidence and holding property. Which Mississippi restriction does it answer most directly? Which does it fail to address clearly, and what would Congress still need to do?

The override showed Congress could pass a major law over the president’s objection. Does that settle who controls Reconstruction, or can a law still be repealed or ignored? What evidence would you want to see next?

t_ed7244cb5698.prompt: Which statement describes rights that Mississippi’s 1865 laws recognized for Black people?

choices.text: They could vote in state elections and hold office.
They could carry firearms freely and choose any employer.
They could serve on juries and attend public schools.
They could marry legally and own personal property.

t_ed7244cb5698.explanation: The laws recognized rights such as legal marriage and ownership of personal property, even as they imposed racial restrictions.

t_36eaf419cb3a.prompt: Why did many Northerners view the Black Codes as a threat after the Union victory?

choices.text: They saw state laws as ending Congress’s authority over citizenship.
They saw racial restrictions as slavery returning under new names.
They saw the codes as giving freed people equal political power.
They saw the laws as restoring the Union without federal action.

t_36eaf419cb3a.explanation: Many Northerners were angry that Southern governments passed racial restrictions soon after the Union victory and read them as slavery in a new form.

t_0ec7394bb36e.prompt: Which objection did Johnson state in his veto of the Civil Rights Act of 1866?

choices.text: The act intruded on authority held by the states.
The act left citizenship decisions to state governments.
The act delayed citizenship for people born in the country.
The act allowed Southern states to send representatives.

t_0ec7394bb36e.explanation: Johnson argued that the act intruded on state authority. He also objected that Southern states lacked representatives in Congress and that citizenship was granted too quickly.

t_6c01fbce93f2.prompt: Congress overrode Johnson’s veto of the Civil Rights Act in April 1866.

choices.text: True
False

t_6c01fbce93f2.explanation: The Senate overrode the veto on April 6, and the House did so on April 9, 1866.

t_2b57f801adc6.prompt: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 listed the right to give evidence in court. Explain how that guarantee could affect a freed person’s ability to take part in a legal case.
t_2b57f801adc6.answer: It could allow a freed person to testify in court as a witness, giving evidence in a legal case.
t_2b57f801adc6.explanation: Section 1 listed giving evidence among the rights of citizens. The guarantee could let a person participate in court by testifying.

t_4b6e1a83ac66.prompt: The 14th Amendment wrote citizenship and equal protection into the Constitution, yet Mississippi’s 1865 laws had already shown that a state could find ways to treat Black residents differently. Is a constitutional amendment a strong enough answer to that problem, or does it only matter if someone is willing and able to enforce it? Take a side and use evidence from today’s lesson.
followUps: The Reconstruction Acts placed ten Southern states under army commanders. Does that show that Congress thought the amendment’s words were not enough by themselves? What does the choice tell us?
Which institution, Congress, the president, the army or the courts, had the most power to make the equal protection clause real in 1867? What is your evidence?
Suppose a state treated people unequally but wrote its law without naming race. Would the clause still apply? How could you decide?

t_9138639e0844.prompt: Congress passed the Reconstruction Acts over Johnson’s vetoes, and the House later impeached him, though the Senate acquitted him by one vote. Was Congress right to take control of Reconstruction from the president, or did it go too far? Defend your view with evidence, including the argument Thaddeus Stevens made.
followUps: Stevens treated the South as conquered land. Is that a fair way to decide who sets the terms? How might Johnson have answered him?
The House charged Johnson with violating the Tenure of Office Act by removing Stanton without Senate approval. Does a disagreement over whether a law applies justify impeachment? Why or why not?
Stevens was one side of a dispute, not a neutral witness. How does knowing that change the way you use his speech as evidence?

t_197afc7ac9a8.title: Build a Reconstruction evidence bank
t_197afc7ac9a8.prompt: Start an evidence bank for your document-based essay by collecting two details that could help you judge what Reconstruction changed and whether it failed. Use your class notes and the handouts from class so far. Paraphrase each detail and explain what it might show; do not write the essay yet.
steps: Choose one detail about a constitutional change or a requirement for Southern states to rejoin the Union. Write where it comes from, for example “14th Amendment, Section 1” or “class notes on the Reconstruction Acts”.
Choose one detail about the conflict between Congress and President Johnson. Write where it comes from, for example “Stevens, speech of December 18, 1865”.
For each detail, write one sentence explaining how it could support or complicate the claim that Reconstruction failed.

t_26aa25ea7640.prompt: Which statement best paraphrases the citizenship clause of the 14th Amendment?

choices.text: People born in a state and eligible to vote are citizens.
People born in the United States to citizen parents are citizens.
People born or naturalized in the United States under its jurisdiction are citizens.
People naturalized by a state and owning property are citizens.

t_26aa25ea7640.explanation: The citizenship clause makes people born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to its jurisdiction, citizens.

t_b91777d59144.prompt: A state charges Black residents a special fee to file a civil lawsuit but charges other residents no fee. Which part of the 14th Amendment most directly challenges this rule?

choices.text: The citizenship clause, because it defines who is a citizen.
The equal protection clause, because the state applies its law unequally.
Section 3, because it limits some former officials from holding office.
The Reconstruction Acts, because they placed states under army commanders.

t_b91777d59144.explanation: The equal protection clause bars a state from denying any person the equal protection of its laws.

t_60e2b794cc16.prompt: Which states were placed together in the third military district under the Reconstruction Acts?

choices.text: Mississippi, Alabama, and Louisiana
North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia
Arkansas, Louisiana, and Texas
Georgia, Alabama, and Florida

t_60e2b794cc16.explanation: The third district consisted of Georgia, Alabama, and Florida.

t_32c9953fdcbc.prompt: The 14th Amendment itself required Southern states to let Black men vote as a condition of readmission to the Union.

choices.text: True
False

t_32c9953fdcbc.explanation: The amendment itself set no such condition. The Reconstruction Acts required states seeking readmission to write new constitutions that let Black men vote and to ratify the 14th Amendment.

t_97097e44f858.prompt: Stevens argued that Congress should set the South’s readmission terms because he treated it as conquered land. Explain how his argument supports Congress’s decision to take control of Reconstruction from Johnson.
t_97097e44f858.answer: Stevens’s argument supports Congress taking control because he claimed Congress, rather than the president, had authority to decide the terms for the Southern states’ return.
t_97097e44f858.explanation: Stevens’s speech presents the dispute as one over which branch of government could set readmission terms. His position gives Congress that authority.

t_26f0e49c1b9d.prompt: The 15th Amendment says a state may not deny or abridge the vote “on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.” It does not say every citizen has the right to vote. Was Congress right to write it this narrowly? Take a side: either a narrow rule was the best Congress could pass and ratify in 1869 and 1870, or a broader rule would have protected Black voters better. Use what you marked in the Guaranteed, Left out and Needs enforcement sort to support your view.
followUps: Many Northern states still limited Black voting in 1869. How might that have shaped what Congress felt it could pass?
The amendment did not mention poll taxes, literacy tests or officeholding. Which one gap do you think mattered most, and why?
Section 2 left enforcement to Congress. Is a good rule enough if the people who must enforce it are not committed to it?

t_28df98946479.prompt: Hiram Revels was seated in the Senate in 1870, South Carolina’s 1868 constitution provided for free public schools, and Black delegates helped write new state constitutions. Do these sources prove that Reconstruction succeeded in opening public life to Black Southerners? Argue for or against, using at least two of the sources from today, and say what the sources cannot show.
followUps: What is the difference between a law or plan on paper and a result in practice? Which of today’s sources are closest to each?
Does the success of one person, like Revels, show what happened to most Black Southerners? What other evidence would you want?
If you were writing a claim for the essay, which word is safer for these sources, “opened” or “ensured”? Why?

t_822e84d57969.title: Weigh your Reconstruction evidence
t_822e84d57969.prompt: This ungraded step prepares you for the document-based essay, which asks: Did Reconstruction fail? Use your evidence bank and the three sources handed out with this sheet: Section 1 of the 15th Amendment, Article X of the South Carolina Constitution of 1868, and the Hiram Revels fact card. Bring your finished sheet to class next time.
steps: Add two details to your evidence bank, each from a different one of the three sources, and note the source. Then sort all four details into gains made during Reconstruction and limits or unmet rights.
Choose the detail that most strongly supports your tentative answer. Explain why it is stronger than one other detail.
Write a one-sentence tentative answer and name one kind of evidence you would still need to make it more convincing.

t_82811004fae7.prompt: Which rule did the 15th Amendment establish about voting?

choices.text: The vote had to be given to every adult citizen, regardless of sex.
The vote could not be denied because of race, color, or previous servitude.
The vote could not be denied because of a person’s income or education.
The vote had to be given to every person born in the United States.

t_82811004fae7.explanation: Section 1 names race, color, and previous condition of servitude as grounds that cannot be used to deny or abridge the vote.

t_ef897d6df205.prompt: Congress passed the 15th Amendment in February 1869, and the states ratified it in 1870.

choices.text: True
False

t_ef897d6df205.explanation: The amendment passed Congress in February 1869 and was ratified in 1870.

t_f578721b49cd.prompt: Which voting rule was outside the 15th Amendment’s explicit protections?

choices.text: A rule limiting the vote to men, without mentioning race.
A rule limiting the vote to white men, based on race.
A rule denying the vote because a man had been enslaved.
A rule denying the vote because of a man’s race.

t_f578721b49cd.explanation: The amendment did not mention sex, so it did not guarantee women the vote.

t_dece768bb5e9.prompt: Which example shows a gain in Black political representation at the national level?

choices.text: Hiram Revels was elected governor by South Carolina’s legislature.
Blanche K. Bruce was the first Black person to sit in Congress.
Hiram Revels wrote South Carolina’s free public school provision.
Hiram Revels was elected to the U.S. Senate by Mississippi’s legislature.

t_dece768bb5e9.explanation: Mississippi’s legislature elected Revels to the Senate in 1870. He became the first Black person to sit in Congress.

t_2023da3d7c1b.prompt: A student uses the 15th Amendment alone to claim that Black men could vote everywhere without barriers. In one or two sentences, explain why this source alone cannot prove that claim about what happened in practice.
t_2023da3d7c1b.answer: The amendment shows a rule against denying or abridging the vote because of race, color, or previous servitude, and Section 2 gives Congress enforcement power. The text alone does not show how the rule was enforced or what happened to voters in practice.
t_2023da3d7c1b.explanation: A strong source-based claim distinguishes a legal rule from results in practice and recognizes the role of enforcement.

t_6501c45cf5b3.title: Document-based essay
t_6501c45cf5b3.prompt:
Write an 800–1,000-word essay that answers the question: Did Reconstruction fail? Say what standard you are judging it by, and take a position in a thesis that includes a qualification. Use evidence from at least four documents in the packet. Name each document when you use it, explain what its evidence shows, and answer the strongest counterevidence to your position. Put quoted words in quotation marks and name the document they come from.

The packet holds the documents read in this unit: Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural Address (1865); Oliver O. Howard, Annual Report of the Commissioner of the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands (1866); the 13th Amendment; Laws of Mississippi, 1865 (the Black Code excerpts); the Civil Rights Act of 1866, Section 1; Andrew Johnson, Veto of the Civil Rights Bill (1866); Thaddeus Stevens, speech to the House of Representatives (December 18, 1865); the 14th Amendment, Section 1; the 15th Amendment; Constitution of South Carolina (1868), Article X; Elias Hill and Nathan Bedford Forrest, testimony to the Joint Select Committee of Congress (1871); Rutherford B. Hayes, Inaugural Address (1877).

The essay is due at the start of class one week after the seminar, on paper or through the class site. Late essays lose 5% a day. It counts for 50% of the course grade.

Organize the essay around reasons that support the thesis. For each document, name it and explain what its evidence shows.
Answer the strongest counterevidence: concede what it gets right, then explain how it qualifies your argument.
Revise for clear organization, accurate historical details, and specific links between evidence and claims.

f_498fa55110b2.question: Why did Lincoln’s plan use 10 percent of 1860 voters instead of a majority?
f_498fa55110b2.answer: The goal was to restore loyal state governments quickly and encourage Southerners to accept the end of slavery. The 1860 voters were white men only, so the plan left out Black men and all women. Congress thought 10 percent was too lenient, which led to the Wade-Davis Bill, requiring a majority and a stricter oath. Lincoln pocket-vetoed it in July 1864.

f_0d9e2fef5899.question: Was Andrew Johnson a Republican, and why did his plan favor wealthy planters?
f_0d9e2fef5899.answer: No. Johnson was a Southern Democrat who ran on Lincoln’s 1864 Union ticket. His plan required wealthy Confederates, including anyone with taxable property over $20,000, to apply to him personally for a pardon. Johnson granted thousands of these pardons, so planters regained political power quickly.

f_34c4a355031a.question: Did either plan give freed people the vote or citizenship?
f_34c4a355031a.answer: No. Johnson’s plan required states to abolish slavery and ratify the 13th Amendment, but it did not require voting rights for Black men. Neither plan settled citizenship, voting or land for the four million freed people. Both plans were made by the president alone, without Congress, so who would control Reconstruction was still open.

f_c796b6f701a1.question: Did the Black Codes say “slavery”? Why do people call them slavery by another name?
f_c796b6f701a1.answer: No. Mississippi’s laws named Black people and set racial restrictions, but they did not use the word slavery. Many Northerners saw the same pattern in them: Black adults could be fined for lacking lawful employment and hired out if they could not pay, and Black minors could be bound to employers. This is where the 13th Amendment’s exception clause for punishment for a crime matters.

f_7bbba3932ab7.question: Did the Mississippi laws give Black people any rights at all?
f_7bbba3932ab7.answer: Yes. The laws of November 1865 let Black people own personal property, sue in court and marry legally. They also restricted where and for whom Black people worked, how their children were raised and whether they could own weapons. Johnson’s plan had required no vote or citizenship for Black men.

f_45d000e8ba6e.question: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1866 do, and why did Johnson veto it?
f_45d000e8ba6e.answer: It declared people born in the United States citizens and listed equal rights, including making contracts, giving evidence and holding property. Johnson vetoed it on March 27, 1866. He argued that it intruded on state authority, that the Southern states had no voice in Congress, and that it gave citizenship to freed people too quickly. Congress overrode the veto in April: the Senate on April 6 and the House on April 9.

f_f77697cbc596.question: Did the 14th Amendment give Black men the right to vote?
f_f77697cbc596.answer: No. Section 1 made people born or naturalized in the United States citizens and barred states from denying anyone the equal protection of the laws. It did not guarantee the vote. The Reconstruction Acts required the Southern states to let Black men vote in their new constitutions. A constitutional ban on denying the vote because of race comes next time.

f_0e3e9e5e5fb8.question: Does impeachment mean the president is removed from office?
f_0e3e9e5e5fb8.answer: No. Impeachment is the House’s vote to charge a president. The Senate then holds the trial. The House impeached Andrew Johnson in February 1868 for violating the Tenure of Office Act by removing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton without Senate approval. The Senate acquitted him in May 1868 by one vote, so he stayed in office.

f_4acb93ebd22e.question: Why did Congress divide the South into military districts instead of letting the states rejoin?
f_4acb93ebd22e.answer: Many in Congress believed Johnson’s plan left freed people unprotected, as the Black Codes showed. The Reconstruction Acts of March 1867 placed ten Southern states in five districts under army commanders. To rejoin the Union, each state had to write a new constitution that let Black men vote and had to ratify the 14th Amendment. Tennessee was left out because it had already ratified the amendment.

f_ca6ca233485d.question: Does the 15th Amendment mean every citizen can vote?
f_ca6ca233485d.answer: No. It says the right to vote cannot be denied or abridged on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. It gave no positive right to vote, did not cover women, and did not mention officeholding. It also did not ban literacy tests or poll taxes.

f_8b36d00a67a3.question: If a rule uses neutral wording, is it fair and legal?
f_8b36d00a67a3.answer: Not necessarily. A rule can sound the same for everyone and still be used to exclude Black voters, for example a hard reading test given only to Black applicants. Section 2 left enforcement to Congress, so the open question was who would act when a rule was applied unequally.

f_7af83f9e635b.question: What can Article X and the Revels fact card prove about Reconstruction?
f_7af83f9e635b.answer: Each shows something real but limited. Article X shows a plan for free public schools in South Carolina’s 1868 constitution. The fact card shows one person’s success: Hiram Revels was seated in the Senate on February 25, 1870, by a vote of 48 to 8. Neither shows how many Black men voted or how many children attended school. A strong claim joins two sources and says what each one shows. Use a verb like “opened,” not “ensured.”

f_e010d04bb90b.question: Was the Klan the same as all white Southerners?
f_e010d04bb90b.answer: No. The Klan began in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1865–1866 among former Confederate soldiers and grew into a secret network. Many white Southerners did not join it. Its leaders were white Democrats who wanted to take back political and economic control. Its targets included Black voters and officeholders, white Republicans, teachers of freed people, and Black families who bought land or refused unfair labor terms.

f_83c25f125999.question: If Nathan Bedford Forrest denied belonging to the Klan, why is his testimony still useful?
f_83c25f125999.answer: A witness account is evidence of what the speaker wanted Congress to believe, as well as of what happened. Ask who is speaking, what the person risked or hoped to gain, and who the audience was. Forrest denied membership and downplayed the group, which fits a wish to protect himself and the South from federal action. Historians widely identify him as a Klan leader. Comparing his account with Elias Hill’s, which describes what Hill suffered and risked retaliation to tell, shows how point of view and purpose shape testimony.

f_2d96bfd2f772.question: Did the Enforcement Acts work?
f_2d96bfd2f772.answer: They worked in part. The acts of 1870–1871 made interference with voting and civil rights a federal crime, allowed federal supervision of elections, and let President Grant use the army and suspend habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties in October 1871. Prosecutions broke the Klan in many places by 1872. But groups such as the White League and the Red Shirts used violence openly afterward. In 1876, United States v. Cruikshank limited the government’s power to prosecute private attackers. So the acts were stronger against the Klan as an organization than against the goal of white political control.

f_135310ca282a.question: If Tilden won more popular votes, why did Hayes become president?
f_135310ca282a.answer: Americans elect the president through the Electoral College, not by popular vote. Tilden led the electoral count 184 to 165, but 20 votes from Florida, Louisiana, South Carolina and Oregon were disputed. A 15-member Electoral Commission voted 8 to 7 along party lines to give all 20 to Hayes. That made the final count 185 to 184. Hayes needed all 20 disputed votes. Tilden needed only one.

f_219d348a8028.question: Was the Compromise of 1877 a written deal?
f_219d348a8028.answer: No. It was a set of informal understandings, and historians debate how binding it was. Southern Democrats accepted Hayes as president. Hayes withdrew the remaining federal troops from the statehouses in South Carolina and Louisiana in April 1877. Promises of a Southern cabinet member and federal aid to Southern railroads were also made.

f_55a35daa6485.question: Did the Supreme Court decisions in the Slaughter-House Cases and Cruikshank show that Northerners no longer cared about Reconstruction?
f_55a35daa6485.answer: Not necessarily. The decisions belong under limits on federal power, not loss of will. The Court read the 14th Amendment narrowly. In Cruikshank (1876) it ruled that the amendment limited states, not private individuals, so the Colfax charges failed. These rulings took away tools the federal government might have used. Economic pressure and political retreat, such as the Panic of 1873 and Grant’s decision not to send troops to Mississippi in 1875, are different kinds of evidence about Northern commitment.

f_f91375d642db.question: What counts as a document when I cite one in the seminar?
f_f91375d642db.answer: Name it specifically. Examples are Hayes’s inaugural address, the Mississippi Black Code of 1865, Section 1 of the 14th Amendment, or Elias Hill’s testimony. Saying “the sources show” is a general claim, not a citation. If you have no second document, borrow one from your evidence bank, then say what claim it supports.

f_d390d394eb44.question: What if I change my mind during the seminar, or I agree with a classmate?
f_d390d394eb44.answer: That is a strong move, not a weakness. Good historians concede what the other side gets right, then qualify their thesis. Say which point convinced you and name the document behind it. You can still hold your position in a narrower form. Your exit ticket asks how a classmate’s counterevidence changed or kept your thesis.

f_edbd043e0bb6.question: How is the seminar scored, and what do I do if I am nervous about speaking?
f_edbd043e0bb6.answer: It is scored on four levels: Excellent, Good, Developing and Beginning. You are scored on what you say in the circle. Excellent means naming a document, saying what it shows, and answering a classmate with specific evidence. Good means naming a document but answering classmates only in general terms. Developing is opinion with no document named. Beginning is not speaking, even when invited. One turn of about 30 seconds can earn Excellent. The seminar counts for 20% of the course grade. Prepare your position card and two named documents ahead of time. If you are quiet, expect a direct question about a document you chose. Speak as yourself, never as a historical person.

f_37316f48fe6f.question: Did every freed person get 40 acres and a mule?
f_37316f48fe6f.answer: No. General Sherman’s Special Field Order No. 15 of January 1865 set aside coastal land from South Carolina to northern Florida in 40-acre plots. Most freed people never received land. The Bureau was to manage abandoned land, but President Johnson’s pardons in fall 1865 returned most of it to its former owners.

f_41d55ce64567.question: Does the exception clause mean a person could be forced to work after any arrest?
f_41d55ce64567.answer: No. The clause allows involuntary servitude only “as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted.” The key words are “duly convicted.” An arrest alone is not a conviction. Next time, we will see how some states tried to use this clause.

f_c7ac0bd4d0ab.question: If the Freedmen’s Bureau was part of the government, why couldn’t it protect freed people more fully?
f_c7ac0bd4d0ab.answer: Its power was limited. It had few agents for the area it covered. It depended on the army to enforce its decisions, and on the president’s support. Both were uncertain. Johnson’s land pardons and his February 1866 veto of a Bureau extension bill show how much the Bureau depended on him. Congress passed a revised bill and overrode his veto of that bill in July 1866.
